approaches.name: Pediatric anterolateral approach to the distal tibia
approaches.corridor: Between tibia and fibula in line with fourth metatarsal, through extensor retinaculum with anterior-compartment tendons retracted medially

sources.title: Open versus closed treatment of distal tibia physeal fractures: systematic review

procedure_applications.condition: A displaced lateral or anterolateral physeal/articular fragment requires direct reduction

positioning.text: Position supine on a radiolucent table with the ankle freely mobile and AP, lateral, mortise, and oblique imaging available.

setup.text: Use CT for displaced articular or transitional patterns, confirm swelling has resolved, and plan a physis-respecting reduction and fixation strategy.

surface_landmarks.text: Mark tibial crest, fibula, ankle joint, fourth-metatarsal axis, extensor tendons, and distal tibial physis.

incision.text: Center a straight incision over the fracture between tibia and fibula in line with the fourth metatarsal; tailor length to fragment, implant, and child size.

superficial_interval.text: Raise full-thickness flaps and open extensor retinaculum while protecting superficial sensory branches and extensor tendons.

deep_interval.text: Retract anterior-compartment tendons medially; mobilize peroneus tertius and anterior-compartment muscle only when proximal extension is necessary.

layers.text: Skin, full-thickness flap, extensor retinaculum, anterior-compartment tendon plane, periosteum/capsule, then distal tibial fragment.

structures_encountered.text: Extensor retinaculum, anterior-compartment tendons, peroneus tertius, distal tibial physis, capsule, and anterolateral fragment are encountered.

structures_at_risk.text: Superficial and deep peroneal nerves, anterior tibial vessels, extensor tendons, physis/perichondral ring, fragment periosteum, and articular cartilage are at risk.

danger_zones.text: Minimize periosteal stripping and avoid fixation trajectories that unnecessarily cross the open physis or penetrate joint.

retraction_hazards.text: Retract anterior tendons medially as a protected unit and avoid forceful pressure on deep neurovascular bundle or tenuous skin flaps.

exposure.text: Provides direct access to lateral distal-tibial and anterolateral articular fragments while preserving medial soft tissue.

limitations.text: Medial and posteromedial fragments are not directly visualized and proximal extension increases anterior-compartment dissection.

extensions.text: Extend only enough to mobilize anterior-compartment muscle proximally or add a separate fragment-specific medial/posterior window.

indications.text: Use for distal-tibial fractures extending laterally, particularly a smaller anterolateral fragment whose fracture exits laterally at articular surface.

relative_contraindications.text: Choose anteromedial exposure when a large anterolateral fragment extends toward medial malleolus or when lateral skin is compromised.

implant_implications.text: Use epiphyseal, metaphyseal, or transphyseal fixation only as dictated by skeletal maturity and pattern, minimizing physeal injury and ensuring extra-articular placement.

fluoroscopy_implications.text: Confirm anatomic joint reduction, physeal alignment, limb axis, and implant containment on AP, lateral, mortise, and oblique images.

closure.text: Restore retinaculum, confirm free tendon excursion, obtain hemostasis, and close soft tissue and skin separately without tension.

complications.text: Complications include physeal arrest, angular deformity, leg-length discrepancy, peroneal neuropathy, tendon adhesions, wound problems, infection, stiffness, and arthritis.

bailouts.text: Add a separate small fragment-directed incision when reduction cannot be verified without excessive periosteal or soft-tissue stripping.

questions.question: Which way are extensor tendons retracted?
What fracture morphology favors this approach?
questions.answer: A smaller anterolateral fragment with a lateral articular exit.

questions.question: What biologic structure must be preserved?
questions.answer: The periosteal and physeal blood supply.

approaches.name: Pediatric anteromedial approach to the distal tibia
approaches.corridor: Immediately medial to the intact tibialis-anterior tendon sheath with limited lateral subperiosteal development when required

sources.title: Foot and ankle fractures during childhood: review

procedure_applications.condition: A displaced medial or large anterolateral physeal/articular fragment requires direct reduction

positioning.text: Position supine with a radiolucent support, free ankle motion, and AP, lateral, mortise, and oblique imaging available.

setup.text: Review CT for articular/transitional injury, delay until swelling permits safe flaps, and template reduction and physis-respecting fixation.

surface_landmarks.text: Mark tibialis-anterior tendon and sheath, tibial crest, ankle joint, medial malleolus, physis, and any traumatic wounds.

incision.text: Center a straight incision over fracture along the medial border of tibialis-anterior tendon, tailoring length to fragment, implant, and leg size.

superficial_interval.text: Raise full-thickness flaps and open extensor retinaculum down to periosteum immediately medial to tibialis-anterior tendon.

deep_interval.text: Preserve tibialis-anterior sheath; when needed, develop the plane behind its posterior border and periosteum to reduce a large anterolateral fragment.

layers.text: Skin, full-thickness flap, extensor retinaculum, intact tibialis-anterior sheath, periosteum/capsule, then distal tibial fragment.

structures_encountered.text: Tibialis-anterior tendon/sheath, extensor retinaculum, distal tibial periosteum and physis, capsule, medial and anterolateral fragments are encountered.

structures_at_risk.text: Tibialis-anterior tendon/sheath, saphenous structures, anterior tibial neurovascular bundle laterally, perichondral ring, physis, periosteum, and cartilage are at risk.

danger_zones.text: Leave tibialis-anterior sheath intact and repair any opening immediately; avoid dissection of the perichondral ring and unnecessary physeal crossing.

retraction_hazards.text: Avoid forceful tendon retraction, flap undermining, and broad lateral stripping behind the tendon sheath.

exposure.text: Provides direct access to medial distal-tibial fractures and large anterolateral fragments extending toward medial malleolus.

limitations.text: Far lateral fixation may require a separate small anterolateral incision, and medial distal tibia has little muscular coverage.

extensions.text: Develop limited lateral plane behind tendon sheath or add a separate small anterolateral window for safe fixation.

indications.text: Use for fractures extending medially and large anterolateral fragments whose medial fracture plane approaches medial malleolus.

relative_contraindications.text: Choose anterolateral or posterior exposure when dominant pathology or safer soft tissue lies outside the medial corridor.

implant_implications.text: Use fixation that restores joint and physis while minimizing physeal crossings; place lateral fixation through a separate window if necessary.

fluoroscopy_implications.text: Confirm articular congruity, physeal alignment, limb axis, and implant containment on AP, lateral, mortise, and oblique views.

closure.text: Repair any tendon-sheath injury immediately, restore retinaculum, confirm tendon excursion, and close viable skin without tension.

complications.text: Complications include physeal arrest, angular deformity, leg-length discrepancy, tibialis-anterior adhesions or attrition, wound necrosis, infection, stiffness, and arthritis.

bailouts.text: Add a separate anterolateral window rather than over-dissecting beneath tibialis-anterior sheath to obtain lateral fixation.

questions.question: When is a separate incision useful?
questions.answer: When fixation of a large anterolateral fragment cannot be performed safely through the medial corridor.

questions.question: Why minimize periosteal dissection?
questions.answer: The distal tibia lacks muscle cover and depends on preserved blood supply.

approaches.name: Pediatric antegrade tibial elastic-nail entry approach
approaches.corridor: Paired medial and lateral proximal-metaphyseal cortical entries placed distal to physis and clear of tibial-tubercle apophysis

sources.title: Entry Points For Antegrade Elastic Nailing
Modern management of paediatric tibial shaft fractures: evidence-based update
Elastic intramedullary nailing in unstable fractures of the paediatric tibial diaphysis: systematic review

procedure_applications.condition: An unstable pediatric tibial fracture requires operative fixation with paired antegrade elastic nails

positioning.text: Position supine on a radiolucent table with proximal tibia and entire leg accessible for orthogonal imaging and fracture manipulation.

setup.text: Mark proximal physis and tibial-tubercle apophysis fluoroscopically, select balanced nail diameters, and plan symmetric opposing bends and entries.

surface_landmarks.text: Mark proximal tibial physis, tibial tubercle/apophysis, medial and lateral metaphyseal cortices, fibular head, and anterior-compartment border.

incision.text: Create medial and lateral incisions beginning at planned entries and extending about 2 cm proximally to permit oblique nail insertion.

superficial_interval.text: Dissect directly to medial cortex; laterally retract proximal anterior-compartment muscle laterally and place entry slightly more anterior as needed.

deep_interval.text: Open paired metaphyseal cortices approximately 2 cm distal to proximal physis, avoiding tubercle cartilage, and angle each entry for controlled nail advancement.

layers.text: Skin, medial subcutaneous or lateral muscle-retraction plane, metaphyseal cortex, then medullary canal.

structures_encountered.text: Medial subcutaneous tibia, lateral anterior-compartment muscle, proximal metaphyseal cortex, physis, apophysis, and medullary canal are encountered.

structures_at_risk.text: Proximal tibial physis, tibial-tubercle apophysis, common peroneal nerve near fibular neck, anterior-compartment muscle, skin at nail ends, and distal physis are at risk.

danger_zones.text: Keep both entries distal to proximal physis and clear of tibial-tubercle apophysis; avoid a far-lateral trajectory toward fibular head/common peroneal nerve.

retraction_hazards.text: Retract lateral muscle gently rather than dissecting posteriorly, and protect skin from prominent nail ends.

exposure.text: Provides paired metaphyseal portals for balanced antegrade elastic nails without crossing proximal physis.

limitations.text: Elastic nails provide limited control in highly comminuted, length-unstable, very proximal/distal, or near-mature patterns and commonly irritate entry sites.

extensions.text: Enlarge either incision only enough for safe cortical access or nail retrieval; add a limited fracture window if closed reduction fails.

indications.text: Use for selected unstable pediatric tibial diaphyseal fractures when acceptable alignment cannot be maintained nonoperatively.

relative_contraindications.text: Choose plate, rigid nail in appropriate maturity, or external fixation when fracture location/stability, soft tissue, or patient size makes ESIN control inadequate.

implant_implications.text: Use two balanced elastic nails with symmetric bends and opposing cortical support; leave ends accessible but not prominent beneath skin.

fluoroscopy_implications.text: Verify both entry points below physis, nail progression, fracture length/rotation/alignment, and distal endpoints clear of physis in AP and lateral planes.

closure.text: Confirm nail ends are buried without skin pressure, obtain hemostasis, and close subcutaneous tissue and skin separately.

complications.text: Complications include entry-site irritation, skin breakdown, infection, malalignment, compartment syndrome, delayed union, nail migration, and physeal/apophyseal injury.

bailouts.text: Add a limited reduction incision or change fixation when balanced nails cannot restore and maintain acceptable length, rotation, and alignment.

questions.question: How far below the proximal physis are entries placed?
Why is the lateral entry more anterior?
questions.answer: To account for proximal anterior-compartment muscle coverage.

questions.question: Which cartilage must be avoided?
questions.answer: The proximal tibial physis and tibial-tubercle apophysis.
